chapters.title: Chapter 2: Listed Shares and Equity Mutual Funds

lessons.title: STCG and LTCG on Listed Shares: Rates and the Annual Exemption

body.text: Tax on listed shares comes down to three numbers: 20%, 12.5% and ₹1.25 lakh. Once you know exactly when each one applies, and when none of them do, you stop overpaying and stop guessing.

children.text: Vikram, a 38-year-old marketing head in Chennai, sold some Reliance shares he had held for three years, redeemed part of his equity mutual fund and booked a quick profit on Trent shares bought six months earlier. His total profit was ₹3,70,000. He assumed his tax would be a flat percentage of that. It was not, and by the end of this lesson you will be able to compute his exact bill yourself.
Two Sections, Two Rates

markDefs.definition: A tax levied on buying and selling securities on a recognised Indian stock exchange, collected by your broker. Paying STT is the condition for the concessional equity capital gains rates under sections 196 and 198 of the 2025 Act.

children.text: For listed equity, the Income-tax Act, 2025 has two special-rate sections. Both apply only where
securities transaction tax (STT)
has been paid.
Section 196 (old 111A):
short-term gains on listed equity shares, equity-oriented mutual fund units and business trust units, taxed at a flat 20%.
Section 198 (old 112A):
long-term gains on the same assets, taxed at 12.5% only on the amount above ₹1.25 lakh in a tax year.

body.text: The STT-on-purchase condition sounds scary, but shares you get through an IPO, bonus issue, rights issue, ESOP allotment, gift or inheritance fall under notified exceptions. In practice, almost every retail investor holding shares through Zerodha, Groww or Upstox meets the condition.

children.text: How the Rates Got Here

body.title: Listed Equity Capital Gains Tax Rates Over Time

children.text: When STT arrived in October 2004, long-term gains on listed equity became fully exempt and short-term gains were taxed at 10%. The STCG rate rose to 15% from April 2008. From April 2018, long-term gains above ₹1 lakh became taxable at 10%. On 23 July 2024, the rates moved to 20% and 12.5%, and the exemption rose to ₹1.25 lakh. The Income-tax Act, 2025 carried these rates over unchanged.
How the ₹1.25 Lakh Exemption Really Works

body.latex: \text{LTCG Tax} = 12.5\% \times \max\big(0,\ \text{Total Section 198 LTCG in the Tax Year} - ₹1{,}25{,}000\big)
body.caption: The exemption applies once to your combined long-term gains from listed shares, equity funds and business trust units for the whole tax year.

children.text: One exemption per person per year,
not per stock, per broker or per fund.
Use it or lose it:
any unused part does not carry forward to the next year.
Long-term only:
short-term gains get no exemption at all.
Equity only:
it does not apply to long-term gains on gold, property or unlisted shares.

body.title: Test the Exemption Rules
body.question: Which statement about the ₹1.25 lakh LTCG exemption is correct?
options: Each stock you sell gets its own ₹1.25 lakh exemption
If you use only ₹50,000 this year, ₹75,000 carries forward to next year
It applies to your total long-term gains on listed shares and equity funds for the tax year
It also reduces short-term gains taxed at 20%
body.explanation: The exemption is a single annual threshold against your combined long-term gains taxed under section 198. It is not per stock, it does not carry forward and it never applies to short-term gains.

body.title: Divya's LTCG Tax
body.prompt: Divya's only capital gains in tax year 2026-27 are ₹2,00,000 of long-term gains from selling Nifty 50 index fund units. Her salary income is well above the basic exemption limit. What is her LTCG tax before cess, in rupees?

children.text: Why 80C and the ₹12 Lakh Rebate Do Not Help Here

Two things surprise salaried investors every year. First, deductions like section 80C (under the old regime) cannot be set off against gains taxed under sections 196 and 198. Second, the rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free under the new regime (section 87A of the 1961 Act) is not available against tax on these special-rate gains. The Finance Act, 2025 made that explicit, and the position continues under the 2025 Act.

body.title: Sanjana's "Tax-Free" Income
body.scenario: Sanjana, a resident in Jaipur, is in the new tax regime. Her taxable salary after the standard deduction is ₹9,00,000. She also has ₹2,00,000 of short-term gains on listed shares. Her total income is ₹11,00,000, below ₹12 lakh, so she assumes she will pay no tax.
body.prompt: Is she right? Work out what she actually pays.
body.modelAnswer: No. The slab tax on her ₹9,00,000 salary is ₹30,000, which the rebate fully wipes out. But the rebate cannot be used against special-rate tax. Her STCG is taxed at 20% under section 196: ₹2,00,000 × 20% = ₹40,000, plus 4% cess, so she pays ₹41,600. Had the same ₹2,00,000 been a long-term gain instead, only ₹75,000 would have been taxable after the exemption, for tax of ₹9,375 before cess.

body.title: Low Income? The Basic Exemption Limit Can Absorb Gains

children.text: If you are a resident individual and your other income is below the basic exemption limit, the unused part of that limit can be set off against your section 196 or 198 gains. This helps students, homemakers, retirees and first-jobbers. Non-residents do not get this benefit.

When Share Gains Do Not Get These Rates

columns.label: Taxed Under Sections 196 and 198
points: Delivery-based buying and selling of listed shares on NSE or BSE
Redeeming or selling equity-oriented mutual fund units
Selling equity ETFs like Nifty BeES on the exchange
Investors holding shares as investments, even with occasional short-term trades

columns.label: Taxed Differently
points: Intraday equity trades: speculative business income at slab rates
Futures and options: non-speculative business income at slab rates
Listed shares sold off-market without STT: short-term at slab rate, long-term at 12.5% under section 197 without the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
High-frequency, systematic trading that the Assessing Officer treats as a business

body.title: Intraday Is Not a Capital Gain
body.textWithBlank: Profits from buying and selling shares on the same day without taking delivery are taxed as ___ business income at your slab rate.
body.explanation: Intraday equity trades are speculative transactions, so profits are speculative business income, not capital gains. Futures and options are non-speculative business income. Neither gets the 20% or 12.5% rates.

body.text: If you both invest and trade actively, keep the two clearly separate. A CBDT circular from 2016 lets investors treat listed shares held for more than 12 months as capital gains if they choose to, but that choice must be applied consistently in later years. Mixing up treatments year to year invites scrutiny.

cards.definition: Old 111A. STCG on listed equity, equity fund units and business trust units with STT, at 20%.
Old 112A. LTCG on the same assets above ₹1.25 lakh a year, at 12.5%.
One annual threshold on total section 198 LTCG. Not per stock, not carried forward, not for STCG.
Securities transaction tax. Its payment unlocks the concessional equity rates.
Surcharge on section 196 and 198 gains cannot exceed 15%, even for very high incomes.
The new-regime rebate for income up to ₹12 lakh cannot be used against tax on special-rate capital gains.

body.title: Your Listed Equity Tax Check Before 31 March
steps: Download your broker's tax P&L and separate short-term and long-term equity gains
Add long-term gains from equity mutual fund redemptions using your CAS
Compare total long-term gains with the ₹1.25 lakh exemption to see how much headroom is left
Confirm none of your "capital gains" are actually intraday or F&O profits
If your other income is low, check how much unused basic exemption limit is available
Estimate tax on gains so you can include it in your advance tax instalments

points: Short-term gains on listed equity with STT are taxed at 20% under section 196 (old 111A)
Long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% under section 198 (old 112A), only above ₹1.25 lakh in total per tax year
The exemption is annual, not per stock, and it does not carry forward
80C-type deductions and the new-regime rebate cannot reduce tax on these special-rate gains
Residents with low other income can use their unused basic exemption limit against these gains
Intraday, F&O and off-market deals without STT fall outside these rates
